 TUTORING  SERVICES FOR 2023

 PURPOSE:  To hear a request to provide a new agreement between the City of Sorith Gate ("City")
 and Southeast Community Foundation ("SCF") ("Agreement")  to provide tutoring services at three (3)
 South Gate Schools for spring, summer and fall semesters.

 RECOMMENDED  ACTION:  The City Council will consider:

  A. Appropriating  $375,000 in American Rescue Plan Act ("ARPA")  funds for an agreement with
  the Southeast Community  Foundation ("SCF") to continue tutoring services  for the spring,
  suininer and fall sessions at three (3) sites in Sorith Gate and internal costs for monitoring  the
  agreement  by staf:f;
  B, Approve agreement with SCF for the tutoring program as outlined in Attacbment A (Scope of
  Work) in an amount not to exceed $345,171; and
  C. Authorize the Mayor to sign an agreement with SCF in a form acceptable to the City Attorney.

 FISCAL  IMPACT:  No General Fund Impact.  All  costs would  be funded by ARPA  within  the
 $375,000.

 ANALYSIS:  SCF has previously reported on their successfiil 5-week summer tutoring program,
 Recently, they completed the fall session of the initial pilot program the City Council funded at the
 May 24, 2022, City Council meeting. The program included a 5-week summer program at one school
 and a 14- week fall program at 2 school sites for $165,000. The goal during the pilot program was to
 reach 30 students in summer and 60 students in the fall semester session.

 During this 5-week summer session, 30 students were enrolled in the program. A total of 28 students
 completed the tutoring pilot program.  Each student was given a diagnostic test to determine the
 current level of proficiency so that at the conclusion, it could be determined how much the tutoring
 assisted. SCF previously presented those results at a November City Council meeting.

 During the fall session, SCF utilized two sites over a 12-week period and served 52 students. On
 average, the students received 20 hours of tutoring assistance during that time period. Date reflects

  I

  310
 that  students  made  progress  in advancement  as shown  between  the pre-level  and post-level  testing
administered.

The new  proposal  would  host  tutoring  services  at three  sites,  of which  two  worild  be at a LAUSD
facility  and the third  could  be at either  a LAUSD  facility  or Aspire  school  site (Charter  School).  All
participating  students  would  need to show  proof  of residency  within  the City  to be eligible  for the
tutoring  services  offered  by SCF.

Many  students  have suffered  significantly  as a result  of the COVID  pandemic.  In many  communities
this impact  was greater  due to many  factors.  Some include  a Lack of financial  resources  to participate
in private  tutoring  services,  lack  of technology  to adequately  participate  in education,  and insufficient
time for parents/legal  guardians  to assist children  with  reading  and math.

SCF will  be making  a short presentation  on what  occurred  during  the fall  semester  session.  In initial
results,  it does strongly  suggest  that these services  have been beneficial  in keeping  students  on  track
with  skills  set appropriate  for their  level  of education.

BACKGROUND:  At the May  24, 2022,  City  Council  meeting,  the City  Council  approved  a $165,000
program  with  the Southeast  Community  Foundation  to provide  tutoring  assistance  for 30 students  at an
elementary  school  site and a 14-week  fall  program  for  60 students  at 2 school  sites.  The tutoring
program  would  supply  1:1 or 1:2 tutoring  to student  ratios  and provide  each student  with  a minimum
of 120 minutes  of tutoring  during  the summer  program.  Each student  received  a diagnostic  assessment
at the start of the program.

By providing  this  critical  program,  the overall  goal is to not only  ensure  that at a minimum  students
maintain  their  current  proficiency  in English  and Math  but  also increase  their  proficiency  levels  in
these two critical  academic  areas.

 PROPOSAL: 2023 SOUTH GATE TUTORING PROGRAM
SCOPE OF WORK

A. BACKGROUND
We already know that the pandemic exacerbated existing inequities in American education, widening
racial and economic gaps in learning. Recent test scores further indicate that the pandemic has
negatively impacted the academic progress of many students. Studies have shown that the pandemic
has left the country’s youth with increased emotional problems, social withdrawal, anxiety and
depression. Moreover, research indicates that nearly two years of remote learning has set many
students back in math and language skills.

The setbacks could have powerful consequences for a generation of children who must move beyond
basics in elementary school to thrive later on.

Suggested solutions to address this learning loss — such as high-dosage tutoring — helps get students
back on the right track. Over the summer and fall of 2022, through support and investment from the
City of South Gate, the Southeast Community Foundation (SCF) was able to implement a pilot program
and make tremendous strides with its resident youth by helping to bridge the education gap that existed
due to almost two years of learning loss and the social emotional needs created by the pandemic. We
have the data to back it all up.

With the continued support and investment from the City of South Gate, we can reach many more
students and help curb learning loss, tracking and understanding the severity and impacts of learning
loss, and then helping student youth get back on track at or above grade level.

B. PURPOSE
The purpose of continuing to expand this tutoring initiative is to provide free, high-quality, in-person
high-dosage tutoring in the subject areas of English Language Arts and mathematics for ninety (90)
underserved, at-risk student youth participating in spring and fall after-school programs, as well as a
summer program, respectively, held at three (3) designated K-12 LAUSD and Aspire school sites within
the City of South Gate, for a combined total of two-hundred seventy (270) students. The Southeast
Community Foundation (SCF) remains as the primary tutoring provider, and will be offering these
services in partnership with Innovate Public Schools (offering back-end administrative support and
managing the collaborative project).

Funds are only to be utilized to prioritize and place underserved, at-risk City of South Gate residents and
youth. SCF will follow the same process and determination of eligibility for participants in this tutoring
program as it did in the summer and fall of 2022 by requesting that the student(s) served to show proof
of residency. We do this by verifying that parent(s) provide a copy of a current utility bill and a current
report card of the student(s).

  350
  C. DESCRIPTION OF SERVICES

 Our high-impact academic enrichment tutoring program focuses on English Language Arts (reading and
 writing) and mathematics, providing each student with an individual assessment of their education level,
 an academic plan and 1:1 to small group tutoring to bring the students skills in line academically to
 grade level or above, meeting California Core Standards. It is the first and only fully-integrated approach
 in our region that improves any school's curriculum and instruction while it provides the right students
 with the right support at the right time. Our tutoring program utilizes tutors that are credentialed
 teachers who work closely with the child’s teachers and family. Our tutors must have a valid California
 teaching credential, must pass a background check, be fully vaccinated, get a TB test, and each receive
 thorough training for the program and compliance. SCF pays for all of these requirements.

 Research shows that high-dosage tutoring is capable of doubling or even tripling what students learn in
 a year. Our tutoring programs have directly demonstrated significant gains in student learning through
 our tracking of student data and have characteristics that have proven to accelerate student learning.
 Characteristics often include: substantial time each week of required tutoring, sustained and strong
 relationships between students and their trained tutors, close monitoring of student knowledge and
 skills, alignment with school curriculum, and support to tutors to assure quality interactions.

D. DELIVERABLES AND TIMELINE FOR SERVICES
 Over 25 weeks, 3,600 hours of free, high-dosage, one-to-one or small group tutoring will be provided to
 270 students in LAUSD and Aspire Public Schools located within the City of South Gate.

 FEATURES OF SOUTH GATE’S TUTORING PROGRAM

  1. 25 weeks of tutoring, over three (3) sessions:
  a. Spring 2023: 10 weeks of tutoring (2x/week) for up to 90 students at 3 school sites (30
  students per site)
  b. Summer 2023: 5 weeks of tutoring (M-Th) for up to 90 students at 3 school sites (30
  students per site)
  c. Fall/Winter 2023: 10 weeks of tutoring (2x/week) for up to 90 students at 3 school sites
  (30 students per site)
  2. Assign 5 tutors, per site, to tutor students in-person
  3. Assign 1 site coordinator, per site, to serve as liaison to school and parents
  4. Tutor to student ratios will be 1:1, up to 1:3
  5. Each participating student receives 120 minutes of tutoring per week (see sample schedule
  below for potential breakdown)

  2
  351
 KEY FEATURES OF SCF’S TUTORING PROGRAM MODEL THAT WILL BE INCORPORATED:

  1. Tutors are certified, credentialed teachers
  2. Students complete a pre- and post-diagnostic assessment in English and Mathematics
  3. Tutors use results of diagnostic assessment to set academic goals and design lesson plans for
  tutoring sessions
  4. Tutoring sessions are frequent (2-4 times per week) and consistent (student has the same tutor)
  5. Grades served: Kindergarten through 12th grade

 E. CONDITIONS OF WORK AND PLACE OF PERFORMANCE

All tutoring sessions will be traditional in-person and on-site at LAUSD and Aspire school sites or a
combination thereof. During the Spring 2023 session, SCF will provide tutoring services at 3 LAUSD
and/or Aspire after school program sites in South Gate. During the Summer 2023 session, SCF will again
provide tutoring services at 3 LAUSD and/or Aspire school sites in South Gate, Monday through Thursday,
in the morning until midday. It may be a combination of the two school sites. For the Fall/Winter 2023
session, tutoring sessions will be in person and on-site at 3 LAUSD and/or Aspire after school program
sites. The specific sites have not yet been determined.

Students will be selected on a first come, first served basis and will be required to commit to the services
for the entire 10 weeks in the Spring and Fall/Winter sessions, and 5 weeks in the Summer session.
Sessions will be mostly one-to-one, with an opportunity for some small group sessions (up to 3 students
per tutor) based on student needs and assessments.

SCF will be the contracted partner with the City of South Gate, and fully responsible for meeting the
terms and conditions of the agreement with the City. SCF will enter into subcontracts with the other
partners for specific areas of support for this project.

At the end of five  years of rate increases,  the City's  sewer  rate would  be the third  lowest  of the

At this time,  staff  is presenting  the Sewer  Rate  Study  to the City  Council  to obtain  guidance
for  proceeding,  and  not  to  approve  a rate  adjustment.  Implementing  a rate  adjustment
requires  approval  through  the Proposition  218  process.  In order  to increase  the  sewer  fee
rate,  the City  must  engage  in a process  mandated  by the  California  State  Constitution.  In
1996  voters  adopted  Proposition  218,  which  added  Articles  XIII  C and XIII  D to the State
Constitution.  Those  new Articles  say that most  property-related  fees constitute  taxes,  which
may  not be created  or increased  without  certain  public  approvals.  In most  cases,  these  fees
must  be approved  by 2/3  of the voters  in a City  election.  Sewer  fees  are exempt  from  that
election  requirement  but are still  subject  to another  Proposition  218 process  requirement.

In order  for a local  government  to adjust  a sewer  fee, they  must  follow:

  i.  Mailing  a notice  and ballot  to all property  owners  with  fee information  noticing  the
  proposed  increase,  structure,  reasoning,  and time  and place  for the Public  Hearing  on
  the proposed  increase.  Such Public  Hearing  must  also provide  a 45-days'  notice  prior
  to it being  held.

  2.  At  the  Public  Hearing,  the  legislative  body  is to consider  all  testimony  given  and
  accept  all  protests  filed  on the  matter.  If  opposing  the  fee  increase,  the  property
  owners  may  submit  the provided  ballot,  another  form  of written  notice,  or testify  at
  the  public  hearing.  Communication  other  than  using  the  provided  ballot  needs  to
  contain  the property  owner  name,  parcel  number,  address  and clear  indication  as to
  their  opposition  to the proposed  fee increase  must  be either  verbally  communicated  at
  the public  hearing  or in the written  document  submitted  by an authorized  individual.

  3.  If a majority  protest  does not exist,  the legislative  body  may  then  approve  and adopt
  the rate  increase  by resolution.  A majority  protest  is considered  reached  if there  are
  50%  plus  one opposing.  There  are approximately  15,526  parcels  within  the City  of
  South  Gate.  An  individual/company  may  own  more  than  one parcel  and would  be
  able  to  cast  their  opposition  with  each  individual  parcel.  Overall,  it would  take
  receiving  7,764  votes  in opposition  to a fee increase.  It is important  to note,  that only
  opposition  ballots/statements  cast by the property  owner  or legal  representative  are
  binding.

BACKGROUND:  The  City  owns  and  operates  a municipal  sanitary  sewer  system  which
provides  services  to properties  citywide.  The sewer  system  is comprised  of nearly  120 miles  of
sewer  mainlines,  19,500  sewer  lateral  services  and  2,400  manholes.  The  Public  Works
Department  is responsible  for  the  management  of the  sewer  system.  The  maintenance  and
operation  generally  required  daily  staffing,  equipment,  vehicles  and contract  services.

The sewer system  is managed  in accordance  with  the 2006  State requirements  which  are outlined
in  the  State  Water  Resources  Control  Board  Order  No.  2006-0003-DWQ  titled  Statewide
General  Waste  Discharge  Requirements  for  Sanitary  Sewer  Systems  (State  Order).  The  State
Order  standardizes  the requirements  to facilitate  proper  funding  and management  of sanitary

  433
 sewer systems,  by requiring  a system-specific  Sewer  System  Management  Plan (SSMP).  SSMPs
must include  provisions  to provide  proper  and efficient  management,  operation,  and maintenance
of sanitary  sewer  systems,  while  taking  into  consideration  risk  management  and cost benefit
analysis.  In Section  9 of "D.  Provision,"  the State Order  stipulates  "The  Enrollee  shall  allocate
adequate  resources  for the operation,  maintenance,  and repair  of its sanitary  sewer  system,  by
establishing  a proper  rate structure,  accounting  mechanisms,  and auditing  procedures  to ensure
an adequate  measure  of revenues  and expenditures."

The condition  of the sewer  system  was evaluated  in the 2019  Sewer  Master  Plan (Master  Plan).
The Master  Plan is a comprehensive  capital  needs assessment  of the sanitary  sewer  system.  The
plan identified several priority projects such as repairs to prevent  sewage  spills.  It identified  $3.5
million  in  funds  needed  to  repair  and  upgrade  the  existing  sewer  system,  which  are now
estimated  at over  $4 Million.  However,  the City  has received  ARPA  funds  of which  $600K  are
programmed  for  sewer  improvements  in FY  2022/23.  It is the intent  of staff  to allocate  more
ARPA  funds toward  sewer projects  over the next 18-months  if they can be designed  and bid with
the timelines  stipulated in the federal  regulations.  Initial  estimates  are between  $1.5 million  to
$2.0 million.  Using  these  funds  is assisting  in lowering  the rate increase  needed  to ensure  the
sewer infrastructure  remains  intact.

The  City  established  the  sewer  enterprise  fund  to address  costs  due to the maintenance  and
improvement  of the sewer  system.  Since 1965  the City  has collected  fees from  residents  based
on water  consumption  to contribute  to the maintenance  and operation  of the City's  sewer system.
The  City  is required  to provide  the current  sewer  system  service  and maintain  its continued
operation  throughout  the City.  The sewer  fund  obtains  its revenue  based  on a $0.35  charge  per
100  cubic  feet  of water  or 748  gallons  used  by residents,  businesses  and  industry.  The  last
modification  to the City's  rate was conducted  2010.

There  are three  alternative  scenarios  in the  Sewer  Rate  Study.  Each  alternative  proposes  to
increase  rates as well  as change  the billing  structure.  The current  billing  structure  is a flat sewer
rate  to all  property  types  based  on the usage  of water  (Variable  Rate).  The  proposed  rate
structure  includes  a Fixed  Rate  plus  Variable  Rate.  The  Variable  Rate  proposed  allows  for
residents  to control  their  bill  based on actual  usage. The Fixed  Rate provides  revenue  needed for
the City's  fixed  operating  cost which  remain  the same regardless  of water  usage.  The proposed
billing  structure  allows  for the variable  rate charged  to be less while  still  securing  an equitable
contribution  to the Sewer Fund to fiilly  fiind  the City's  needs.

The rate increase  is proposed  to meet the needs of the sewer  program  over  the next five  years.
The  rates  would  provide  for  eliminating  the  projected  operations  and  maintenance  deficits
previously  shown  in the 5-year  projection.

The  following  tables  include  a summary  of  the  three  alternative  fee  pricing  that  are being
presented.  It should  be noted  that the impact  on all users will  vary  depending  on their  water

  present a project and program that would permit the video/streaming of City Corincil meetings.

  FISCAL  IMPACT:  This is a discussion item and development of direction, if any, to staff. Should

  ANALYSIS:  Vice Mayor Hurtado and City Council Member Barron  have requested  this item  be

  Attached (Exhibit A) are the results of a quick survey of neighboring cities to provide information
  related to the use of cameras to broadcast their meetings.  While only four cities responded to the
  request, it is recognized that nearly all of the 14 cities asked, do video/stream their Council meetings
  and/or other bodies.

  Based on tlie survey and other information,  the act of providing video/streaming  of City Council
  meetings started for a large number prior to COVID, as well as part of the local government  cable
  systetn agreements to provide public, educational, and goverental  (PEG) access channels.  For
  many local governments, the process of providing video was to provide increased transparency of the
  legislative process and the only technology that existed to accomplish that goal. Around early 2012,
  technology became possible to allow ability to listen, see and participate in government process
  through platforms like Zoom and TEAMS.  These types of platforms grew significantly  as a result of
  COVID to allow not only the public, but governmental officials that could not meet in person.

  For most cities that have been using video/streaming, they have a dedicated staff member or members
  for the monitoring and processing of such videos. Even a single camera usually requires an individual

 to monitor  and adjust  as the meeting  proceeds.  With  multiple  cameras,  the need  for a dedicated  person
is a necessity.  Supplementing  the  survey  are the  personal  experiences  of the  City  Manager  in the

CITY OF SOUTH GATE
  REGULAR MEETING AGENDA
  MINUTES
  TUESDAY, MARCH 28, 2023

CALL TO ORDER  Maria del Pilar Avalos, Mayor called a Regular City Council Meeting to
  order at 6:38 p.m.

INVOCATION  Pastor Ernesto Trejo, South Gate Church of Christ

PLEDGE OF
ALLEGIANCE  Salvador Campos, Recreation Coordinator

ROLL CALL  Yodit Glaze, City Clerk

PRESENT  Mayor Maria del Pilar Avalos, Vice Mayor Gil Hurtado, Council Member
  Joshua Barron, Council Member Maria Davila, and Council Member Al
  Rios; City Manager Chris Jeffers, City Attorney Raul F. Salinas

ABSENT  City Treasurer Jose De La Paz

1
CD/HOUSING  The City Council unanimously approved A and B by motion of Council
  Member Rios and seconded by Mayor Avalos.

  a.  Resolution No. 2023-15-CC entitled - A Resolution of the City
  Council of the City of South Gate, California approving
  Substantial Amendment No. 1 to the FY 2021-2022 Annual Action
  Plan approving the HOME-ARP Allocation Plan due to HUD by
  March 31, 2023; and authorizing the City Manager, or designee, to
  submit to HUD, in a form approved by the City Attorney; and

  b.  Appropriated $387,686 from the HOME-ARP funds to an account
  determined by the Director of Administrative Services to fund the
  administration of the HOME-ARP program.

  ROLL CALL: Council Member Baron, yes; Council Member Davila,
  yes; Council Member Rios, yes; Vice Mayor Hurtado, yes; Mayor Avalos,
  yes.

  Carol Averell, Housing Manager, provided a presentation on this item.

  Council Member Hurtado asked if there are any numbers showing how
  many are at risk of becoming homeless.

  Ms. Averell stated that the money has already been allocated from HUD
  and they do follow a formula that is based on the population of the city.

  Mayor Avalos asked if there could be a map that shows which areas of
  South Gate would fall under these qualifications.
   REGULAR CITY COUNCIL MEETING MINUTES OF MARCH 28, 2023

i
CD/HOUSING CONT'D  Chris Jeffers, City Manager stated that at this point we are designating
  which programs the funding will be used for. The city will need a process
  to verify income to see if applicants qualify and review what exactly the
  program allows.

  Mayor Avalos opened the public hearing and asked if anyone in the
  audience wishes to speak on this item. Seeing no come forward, Mayor
  Avalos closed the public hearing.

  Council Member Baron clarified that this item is to accept the allocation
  of funds.

  Ms. Averell stated that Council Member Baron is correct, and that the
  distribution of funds will come later.

DEVIATE FROM
THE AGENDA  At this time, there being no objections, Mayor Avalos stated that item 12
  would be considered out of its regular agenda order.

12
WASTEWATER MGMT  The City Council received and filed the presentation on the Sewer Rate
  Study. The City Council requested that staff bring back information on
  Option No. 2 (5-year Financial Plan Revenue Adjustment) by motion of
  Mayor Avalos and seconded by Council Member Hurtado.

  a.  Received and filed a presentation on the Sewer Rate Study; and

  b.  Provided the City Manager with direction on next steps, if any, as
  it relates to the fiscal sustainability of the City's Sewer Fund.

  ROLL CALL: Council Member Baron, yes; Council Member Davila,
  yes; Council Member Rios, yes; Vice Mayor Hurtado, yes; Mayor Avalos,
  yes.

DEVIATE FROM
THE AGENDA  At this time, there being no objections, Mayor Avalos stated that item 2
  would be considered out of its regular agenda order.

2
STREETS/SIDEWALKS/
LANDSCAPING  The City Council adopted Resolution No. 2023-16-CC entitled - A
  Resolution of the City Council of the City of South Gate, California
  declaring an emergency still exists and authorizing repair, replacement or
  maintenance activities of public facilities related to the Urban Orchard,
  City Project No. 539-PRK, without public bidding, pursuant to the
  emergency contracting procedures of the South Gate Municipal Code and
  the California Public Contract Code by motion of Council Member Barron
  and seconded by Council Member Davila

  Page 2 of 9
   REGULAR CITY COUNCIL MEETING MINUTES OF MARCH 28, 2023

2
STREETS/SIDEWALKS/
LANDSCAPING CONT'D  ROLL CALL: Council Member Baron, yes; Council Member Davila,
  yes; Council Member Rios, yes; Vice Mayor Hurtado, recused; Mayor
  Avalos, yes.

DEVIATE FROM
THE AGENDA  At this time, there being no objections, Mayor Avalos stated that item 5
  would be considered out of its regular agenda order.

5
PARKS  The City Council approved A and B by motion of Council Member Barron
  and seconded by Council member Davila

  a.  Amendment No. 1 to Contract No. 3485 with David Volz Design
  (DVD) to extend the term of the contract through June 30, 2024,
  and to provide design and construction support services on the
  Circle Park Renovation Project, City Project No. 609-PRK, for an
  amount not to exceed $99,085; and

  b.  Authorized the Mayor to execute Amendment No. 1 in a form
  acceptable to the City Attorney.

  ROLL CALL: Council Member Baron, yes; Council Member Davila,
  yes; Council Member Rios, yes; Vice Mayor Hurtado, recused; Mayor
  Avalos, yes.

DEVIATE FROM
THE AGENDA  Mayor Avalos provided her report before having to leave the City Council
  Meeting.

  Mayor Avalos attended that AltaMed recognition by Congresswoman
  Barragan presenting a check for 2.5 million dollars for their residency
  program. She also participated in making a video with Council Member
  Rios in support of mental health and the Multi-Cultural Woman's Club
  Women's Day acknowledgement. The County Sanitation District will
  host an Earth Day Event on April 22 in Whittier.

EXCUSED FROM
MEETING  At 7:51 p.m., Mayor Avalos was excused from the meeting and departed
  from the Council Chambers.

COMMENTS FROM
THE AUDIENCE  Amy Lu, Leland Weaver Community Library shared information about
  the Reading Stars program.

  Andrea asked if Code Enforcement checks the placement of residential
  trash cans and overgrown lawns.

  Page 3 of 9
   REGULAR CITY COUNCIL MEETING MINUTES OF MARCH 28, 2023

COMMENTS FROM
THE AUDIENCE CONT'D  Mario Dominguez requested that at the April 13th Parks and Recreation
  Meeting would like to place the mural project on the agenda including and
  emailing the public photos of the sample art.

  Bash, Tweedy Mile Association thanked the City Council and Staff for
  their support of the Azalea Festival Car Show.

  Thomas Buckley supported the decision of the city to close the carnival on
  Friday night but does disagree with the closure on Saturday and Sunday.
  He stated that the city did a poor job of communicating with the
  community as to what was going on.

  Ana, Chamber of Commerce invited everyone to attend a meet and greet
  with the Mayor on April 1st. She also encourages everyone to check out
  the gift card program that is continuing. There are about 25 businesses
  that are participating in the program and the city is matching the amount
  purchased for each card.

  Cyndi Esquivel stated that if the carnival was shut down due to public
  safety, she agrees with the decision, but the city didn't communicate the
  reasons with the community.

REPORTS AND COMMENTS
FROM CITY OFFICIALS  Meredith Elguira, Director of Community Development, reported that City
  received a grant for the site assessment at 13050 Paramount Blvd. Last
  week was Co Op with Code for the cleanup of the United Pacific Railroad
  tracks.

  Steve Costley, Interim Director of Parks and Recreation, reported on the
  Azalea Festival events. Since the beginning of 2021 the city has hosted a
  COVID testing site at South Gate Park. Los Angeles County has decided
  to close many of these testing sites and March 31st will be the last day for
  this site.

  Kris Ryan, Director of Administrative Services, reported that the Finance
  Department is moving forward with the budget and should have an item
  coming before the Council shortly.

  Jon Hamilton, Director of Human Resource announced the open positions
  for the City of South Gate.

  Darren Arakawa, Chief of Police, received a 26-foot DUI trailer from the
  Office of Traffic Safety by a grant awarded to the city. Baker to Vegas
  run starts next weekend.

  Chris Jeffers, City Manager, reported that on Friday night at the carnival
  approximately 150 teens became unruly, in fact, 1 juvenile was arrested
  with a gun. The situation escalated and the city could no longer guarantee
  Page 4 of 9
   REGULAR CITY COUNCIL MEETING MINUTES OF MARCH 28, 2023
REPORTS AND COMMENTS
FROM CITY OFFICIALS  the safety of participants at the event. The event ended at 9:30 p.m. a half
  an hour before the scheduled time. The decision to close the carnival on
  Saturday and Sunday was based on the number of available staff that the
  city could provide on short notice. The City Managers priority is that the
  community is safe.

  Mr. Jeffers explained that Mr. Dominguez did have the opportunity to
  address the Parks and Recreation Commission regarding the graffiti style
  writing being suggested for the mural. There was a presentation by TPL
  that included pictures. Mr. Dominguez did address the commission both
  orally and in writing. The Commission is made up of 5 residents and they
  reached the decision that the general painting was good, but the style of
  lettering was not appropriate and requested that additional fonts be
  presented.

  Yodit Glaze, City Clerk reported that she attended the Multi-Cultural
  Women's Club conference. She was a judge for the Miss Azaelita
  Contest, the Miss South Gate Pageant, and the Azalea Festival Car Show.

  Council Member Davila thanked the participants of the Multi-Cultural
  Women's Club conference, the Miss South Gate Pageant, and the Miss
  Azaelita Contest. Council Member Davila supported the decisions of the
  City Staff to close the carnival.

  Council Member Barron supported the decisions of the City Staff to close
  the carnival but was glad to have these conversations and recognizes that
  the city might have been able to communicate better with the residents.

  Council Member Rios attended the Azalea Festival Car Show and spoke
  on participating in the making of the video for the video in support of
  mental health programs. He supports the decisions of the decisions of the
  City Staff to close the carnival but would like to see us offer more
  programs for youth to take part in.

  Vice Mayor Hurtado spoke about the recent school shooting in Tennessee
  and agrees with staff about closing the carnival. He stated that he received
  messages from people saying that they knew this was going to happen
  because their kids where about it in school and that society tries to excuse
  their behavior by saying there is not enough programs for the youth, but it
  really comes down to family. The Vice Mayor said that the City needs to
  improve communication with the residents and needs to continue to
  enforce our own rules.

CONSENT CALENDAR  Agenda Items 3, 4, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10 and 11 were approved by motion of
  Council Member Rios and seconded by Council Member Barron. Items 2
  and 5 were pulled for separate discussion.

  Page 5 of 9
   REGULAR CITY COUNCIL MEETING MINUTES OF MARCH 28, 2023

CONSENT CALENDAR
CONT'D  ROLL CALL: Vice Mayor Hurtado, yes (recused for Item 9); Council
  Member Davila, yes, (recused for Item 3 and abstain for Item 11), Council
  Member Rios, yes; Council Member Barron, yes; Mayor Avalos, excused.

3
PARKING & TRAFFIC  The City Council approved A and B during the consent calendar.

  a.  Agreement (Contract No. 2023-35-CC) with Fountainhead
  Consulting Corporation (Fountainhead) to provide construction
  management and inspection services for the construction of the
  Tweedy Boulevard Signal Synchronization Project, City Project
  No. 514-TRF, in an amount not to exceed $175,290; and

  b.  Authorized the Mayor to execute the Agreement in a form
  acceptable to the City Attorney.

4
WASTEWATER MGMT  The City Council approved A and B during the consent calendar.

  a.  Amendment No. 1 to Contract No. 2020-53-CC with John L.
  Hunter and Associates, Inc. to extend management services for the
  Industrial Waste Program and Fat, Oil, and Grease Control
  Program for one year, not-to-exceed amount of $56,760; and

  b.  Authorizing the Mayor to execute Amendment No. 1 to Contract
  No. 2020-53-CC in a form approved by the City Attorney.

6
PARKING & TRAFFIC  The City Council approved A, B, C and D during the consent calendar.

  a.  Agreement (Contract No. 2023-36-CC) with Servitek
  Electrical Inc., for the Replacement of Damaged Traffic Signal
  Poles, City Project No. 655-TRF ("Agreement"), in an amount not-
  to-exceed $351,857;

  b.  Appropriated $315,170 in Proposition C Funds to fully fund the
  Replacement of Damaged Traffic Signal Poles, City Project No.
  655-TRF ("Project");

  c.  Notice of Exemption for the Project, pursuant to Title 14 of the
  California Code of Regulations, Existing Facilities Section 15301
  Class and directing the City Clerk to file it with the Los Angeles
  County Registrar Recorder's Office; and

  d.  Authorized the Mayor to execute the Agreement in a form
  acceptable to the City Attorney.

  Page 6 of 9
   REGULAR CITY COUNCIL MEETING MINUTES OF MARCH 28, 2023

7
PERSONNEL - MOU BETW
CITY & EMPLEE GROUPS  The City Council approved A and B during the consent calendar.

  a.  Resolution No. 2023-17-CC entitled Resolution of the City
  Council of the City of South Gate, California, approving
  the SGMEA MOU (Contract No. 2023-37-CC) and the SGPMMA
  MOU (Contract No. 2023-38-CC) for the term of July 1, 2021,
  through June 30, 2024; and

  b.  Authorized the Mayor to execute the comprehensive successor
  Memorandums of Understanding in a form acceptable to the City
  Attorney.

8
PERSONNEL RECRUITMENT
& SELECTION  The City Council adopted Resolution No. 2023-18-23 entitled Resolution
  of the City Council of the City of South Gate, California, amending
  Resolution No. 6454 (Salary Resolution and Position Classification Plan)
  by approving the job classification specifications for the following
  positions during the consent calendar.

  a.  Electrical Supervisor;

  b.  Facilities Maintenance Specialist;

  c.  Facilities Maintenance Technician II;

  d.  General Maintenance Foreman;

  e.  Water Distribution Foreman;

  f  Water Distribution Operator I;

  g.  Water Distribution Operator II;

  h.  Water Lead Worker;

  i.  Water Meter Reader II;

  j.  Water Operations Foreman;

  k.  Water Pump Operator I;

  1.  Water Pump Operator II; and

  m.  Water Quality & System Lead Operator.

  Page 7 of 9
   REGULAR CITY COUNCIL MEETING MINUTES OF MARCH 28, 2023

9
SCHOOLS/EDUCATION  The City Council approved A, B and C during the consent calendar.

  a.  Appropriated $375,000 in American Rescue Plan Act ("ARPA")
  funds for an agreement with the Southeast Community Foundation
  ("SCF") to continue tutoring services for the spring, summer and
  fall sessions at three (3) sites in South Gate and internal costs for
  monitoring the agreement by staff;

  b.  Agreement (Contract No. 2023-39-CC) with SCF for the tutoring
  program as outlined in Attachment A (Scope of Work) in an
  amount not to exceed $345,171; and

  c.  Authorized the Mayor to sign an agreement with SCF in a form
  acceptable to the City Attorney.

10
LAW ENFORCEMENT  The City Council approved A, B and C during the consent calendar.

  a.  Purchase Order Agreement with ATV Corp for the purchase
  of one Prowler C4XM police off-road utility vehicle for the Police
  Department, in the total amount of $50,340.15;

  b.  Appropriated $2,397.15 from the Asset Forfeiture Fund to cover
  the full cost of the vehicle; and

  c.  Authorized the Mayor to execute the Purchase Order in a form
  acceptable to the City Attorney.

11
MINUTES  The City Council approved A, B, C, D, E, F, G and H during the consent
  calendar.

  a.  The Regular Meeting minutes of November 22, 2022;

  b.  The Recessed Meeting minutes of November 29, 2022;

  c.  The Regular Meeting minutes of December 13, 2022;

  d.  The Special Meeting minutes (Closed Session) and Special
  Meeting Minutes of January 10, 2023;
